figures.name: Eliezer Yudkowsky
figures.role: Co-founder, Machine Intelligence Research Institute (MIRI); co-author of 'If Anyone Builds It, Everyone Dies' (2025) — as of Sept 2026
figures.bio: Eliezer Yudkowsky is an American AI researcher and writer who co-founded the Machine Intelligence Research Institute (MIRI) and has argued since the early 2000s that aligning superhuman AI is the central problem of the century. His 2025 book with Nate Soares, 'If Anyone Builds It, Everyone Dies', calls for an internationally enforced halt to the development of superintelligence.

sources.title: Pausing AI Developments Isn't Enough. We Need to Shut it All Down (TIME op-ed)
sources.note: Indefinite worldwide moratorium on large training runs; shut down GPU clusters; track GPUs; be willing to enforce by airstrike; 'literally everyone on Earth will die'.

sources.title: AGI Ruin: A List of Lethalities
sources.note: 'First critical try'; capabilities generalize further than alignment; 'no idea what's actually going on inside the giant inscrutable matrices'.

sources.title: If Anyone Builds It, Everyone Dies (book, with Nate Soares) — publisher page
sources.note: Little, Brown. Thesis: a superintelligence built with current methods would have goals not ours and 'would crush us'; calls for coordinated halt of large-scale general AI development.

sources.title: Researchers give doomsday warning about building AI too fast (Semafor interview)
sources.note: Complete cessation rather than regulation; even Safe Superintelligence 'should shut down'; building software 'closer to alchemy than science'.
sources.audit: Resolves, but 'should shut down' (Safe Superintelligence) and 'closer to alchemy than science' are the reporter's paraphrases ('according to Yudkowsky and Soares', 'the authors argue'), not direct quotes. d2 and s2 print them inside quotation marks as his word

sources.title: The Ezra Klein Show: How Afraid of the A.I. Apocalypse Should We Be?
sources.note: Long interview on the book; 'we're the ants' analogy; expects every human dies shortly after a too-powerful AI is built under present conditions.

sources.title: AI Governance to Avoid Extinction (MIRI Technical Governance Team)
sources.note: MIRI institutional paper (Barnett & Scher), not Yudkowsky's own text: international 'Off Switch' then coordinated Halt; other trajectories 'carry an unacceptable risk'.

sources.title: Human Augmentation as a Safer AGI Pathway (Dan Faggella interview)
sources.note: Symmetrical treaty between US, China, UK etc.; restrictions on AI R&D; human augmentation as the safer route. Summary page, not full transcript.

sources.title: X post: 'This is not the act that prevents the Earth from being destroyed -- that would take a treaty'
sources.note: Text as indexed by search; X not fetchable by our tool and the post's context (which act he is reacting to) is unclear. Says ASI 'can kill you just as easily from a datacenter running outside your country'.
sources.audit: x.com returns HTTP 402 to automated fetches; could not be opened. The first team's own note says the context of the post is unclear. Do not use as sole support (s4, s5 also rest on TIME, which is sufficient).

sources.title: Audit source
sources.note: Added by the independent audit.

figures.oneLiner: Superhuman AI built with today's methods would kill everyone; the only sane response is a global, enforced halt.

d1.basis: 'The most likely result of building a superhumanly smart AI... is that literally everyone on Earth will die.'

d2.basis: 'We've got no idea what's actually going on inside the giant inscrutable matrices and tensors of floating-point numbers' (AGI Ruin §25). Interpretability cannot yet say whether a system is planning harm.

d3.basis: AGI Ruin, 2022: 'Fast capability gains seem likely, and may break lots of previous alignment-required invariants simultaneously.' A premise he has held since the 2008 AI-Foom debate.

d5.basis: Book thesis: an ASI's goals are 'vanishingly unlikely' to be aligned with human values; 'if it comes to conflict... would crush us'.

d7.basis: Unaligned operation at a dangerous level of intelligence 'kills everybody on Earth and then we don't get to try again' (AGI Ruin §3). No second try means no regaining control afterwards.

d8.basis: 'If we go ahead on this everyone will die'; aligned ASI would be wonderful but he thinks that is not what will be built.

d9.basis: 'Capabilities generalize further than alignment once capabilities start to generalize far' (AGI Ruin §21); alignment is 'not on course' to be solved 'in time on the first critical try'.

s1.basis: 'Shut it all down': indefinite worldwide moratorium, 'no exceptions, including for governments or militaries'.

s2.basis: TIME, 2023: 'anyone talking of arms races is a fool'. AGI Ruin, 2022: a careful lab that holds back only lets another 'destroy the world two years later'.

s3.basis: Wants a hard ceiling on compute, not permits; would likely take licensing as a floor while calling it insufficient ('pausing isn't enough').

s4.basis: International agreements with enforcement, GPU tracking, willingness to 'destroy a rogue datacenter'; 'that would take a treaty'.

s5.basis: Prescriptive version: no, your country should not push ahead; it should seek a treaty.

s6.basis: TIME, 2023: held to the 'standards of engineering rigor that apply to a bridge', 'the entire field would be shut down tomorrow'. 'We are not prepared.' He wants a halt, which goes beyond a safety case.

s7.basis: TIME, 2023: the moratorium 'needs to be indefinite and worldwide'; 'Make immediate multinational agreements to prevent the prohibited activities from moving elsewhere.' Far beyond existing law.

s8.basis: TIME, 2023: solving safety 'could very reasonably take at least half that long' (half of 60 years), and still: 'Shut it all down.' He accepts any delay.

s9.basis: TIME, 2023: 'preventing AI extinction scenarios is considered a priority above preventing a full nuclear exchange'. No lab-scale gamble is acceptable to him.

s10.basis: Lives saved do not outweigh the case for slowing; 'no cure helps anyone if the technology ends us'.

s11.basis: On open-sourcing GPT-4: 'that's just sheer catastrophe. The whole notion of open sourcing, this was always the wrong approach, the wrong ideal' (Lex Fridman #368, 2023). Wants large training runs banned outright.

s13.basis: TIME, 2023: 'Shut down all the large training runs.' And: 'Shut it all down. We are not ready.'

p1.basis: Trusts neither; wants an international regime above both. Governments at least can enforce a halt, companies cannot be trusted to self-limit.

p2.basis: Expects superintelligence possibly within that window (if we survive); stresses timing is uncertain. Inferred from book and interviews.

p4.basis: Sees misaligned AI as the overwhelming danger; concentration is a secondary worry compared with 'everyone dies'.

p5.basis: Thinks GPU tracking makes verification feasible but is pessimistic about political will; no explicit estimate.

d4.basis: He does not bet on LLMs stalling: the book wants a ban on stronger models precisely because the next upgrade could be superintelligence.

d10.basis: 'No idea what's actually going on inside'; developers 'don't understand' what they build.

s12.basis: Not his focus, but consistent with his demand that builders bear responsibility; would call liability far too weak on its own. Inferred.

p3.basis: Long-held view that digital minds can be moral patients (co-wrote 'The Ethics of Artificial Intelligence' with Bostrom); warns against making them casually.

figures.name: Marc Andreessen
figures.role: Co-founder and general partner, Andreessen Horowitz (a16z) — as of Sept 2026
figures.bio: Marc Andreessen co-created the Mosaic browser, co-founded Netscape and in 2009 co-founded the venture firm Andreessen Horowitz, a major investor in AI start-ups. His 2023 essays 'Why AI Will Save the World' and 'The Techno-Optimist Manifesto' argue that accelerating AI is a moral imperative and that fear-driven regulation, not AI, is the danger.

sources.title: Why AI Will Save the World
sources.note: 'AI is math – code – computers'; 'it doesn't want, it doesn't have goals'; AI risk 'a cult'; 'not aware of a single actual bad use for AI that's not already illegal'; 'single greatest risk... China wins'.

sources.title: Marc Andreessen says big companies want a government-protected cartel (Fortune)
sources.note: Licensing = 'fleets of lawyers'; 'you're literally telling people they can't write code and put it on the internet'; 'wolf invited into the henhouse'.

sources.title: The Techno-Optimist Manifesto
sources.note: 'Our enemy is the Precautionary Principle'; 'any deceleration of AI will cost lives'; lists 'existential risk' and 'risk management' among a 'demoralization campaign'; decentralization over central planning.

sources.title: Tech billionaires bicker over open vs. closed AI (Fortune)
sources.note: 'AI isn't nukes, it's math'; open source communities 'should be free to pursue AI'; 'ginned-up moral panic'.

sources.title: The Little Tech Agenda (with Ben Horowitz)
sources.note: Incumbents seek 'regulatory capture – a wall of laws and regulations that protect and entrench their positions'; agencies 'green lit in real time' against AI.

sources.title: Anthropic CEO blasts Andreessen's 'just math' argument (Fortune)
sources.note: Quotes his posts: 'Restricting AI means restricting math, software, and chips'; regulation of AI 'is the foundation of a new totalitarianism'.

sources.title: Marc Andreessen on AI, Tech, Censorship, and Dining with Trump (The Free Press)
sources.note: Says the Biden administration tried to 'control AI' via a few favoured companies; AI censorship 'a million times more dangerous'. Full transcript paywalled.

sources.title: Marc Andreessen's 2026 Outlook: AI Timelines, US vs. China, and The Price of AI (a16z podcast)
sources.note: 'Cost of intelligence is collapsing'; largest tech shift of his life; regulatory fragmentation; open vs closed; China. Page has summary only.

sources.title: a16z's 2026 Outlook by Andreessen Horowitz (36Kr English summary)
sources.note: Secondary, translated: Washington now has 'little interest in doing anything that might prevent us from beating China'; 'thousands of AI bills' in states 'quite scary'; Europe 'kneecapping'.

figures.oneLiner: AI is math built and run by people; the real risks are stagnation, cartels and China winning, not runaway machines.

d1.basis: 'AI doesn't want, it doesn't have goals, it doesn't want to kill you, because it's not alive'; a mind of its own is 'a superstitious handwave'.

d2.basis: Treats AI as software 'built by people, controlled by people'; would say testing and market discipline are the check, as for any complex product.

d3.basis: AI is 'math – code – computers, built by people… controlled by people'; the idea that it will 'develop a mind of its own' is 'a superstitious handwave'. No runaway jump in his model; ordinary software progress.

d5.basis: 'It doesn't have goals'; the idea it 'will develop a mind of its own is a superstitious handwave'.

d7.basis: AI 'is owned by people and controlled by people, like any other technology'; against bad actors, use 'AI as a defensive tool'. The item no longer asks about institutions, so nothing holds him back.

d8.basis: 'Why AI Will Save the World'; 'any deceleration of AI will cost lives'; AI as 'our Philosopher's Stone'.

d9.basis: Denies that AI gets harder to keep safe: it 'doesn't want, it doesn't have goals'. For misuse, 'put AI to work in cyberdefense, in biological defense': defenders gain as fast as attackers. Inferred from stance.

s1.basis: 'Our enemy is deceleration'; a halt is the outcome he has spent three years fighting.

s2.basis: Wants the US and 'little tech' to build fast and win; but frames it as America vs China, not 'the most careful developers first'.

s3.basis: Licensing is the 'government-protected cartel'; 'you're literally telling people they can't write code'.

s4.basis: 'AI isn't nukes, it's math'; a compute treaty is the cartel made global. 'Regulation of AI (math) is the foundation of a new totalitarianism.'

s6.basis: 'Our enemy is the Precautionary Principle'; burden-of-proof regimes are how incumbents lock out competitors.

s7.basis: 'We don't even need new laws – I'm not aware of a single actual bad use for AI that's not already illegal.'

s8.basis: Techno-Optimist Manifesto, 2023: 'any deceleration of AI will cost lives. Deaths that were preventable by the AI that was prevented from existing is a form of murder.'

s9.basis: Rejects the premise of a measurable 1%.

s10.basis: 'Any deceleration of AI will cost lives.'

s11.basis: 'Open source AI should be allowed to freely proliferate and compete with both big AI companies and startups. There should be no regulatory barriers to open source whatsoever.'

s13.basis: 'Our enemy is deceleration'; no deliberate slowing.

p1.basis: 'Wolf invited into the henhouse'; regulators are captured and 'green lit in real time' against AI. Would trust neither, but the agency far less.

p2.basis: Says the cost of intelligence 'is collapsing' and this is the largest shift of his life, yet has long argued AI will not cause mass unemployment. Mixed.

p4.basis: Fears a government-blessed cartel and 'a new totalitarianism' far more than autonomous AI, which he thinks cannot act on its own.

p5.basis: Would expect China (and others) to ignore any pause.

d4.basis: Calls AI 'a universal problem solver' and expects it to keep improving; but denies it is a mind, so 'autocomplete' framing partly fits. No direct statement.

d10.basis: 'Built by people, owned by people, used by people, controlled by people'; he does not claim full interpretability. Inferred.

s12.basis: Fought SB 1047-style developer liability; a16z line: target 'the person or entity primarily responsible' for harm, not toolmakers.

p3.basis: 'It's not alive'; attributing wants or experience to it is 'superstitious'.

figures.name: Guillaume Verdon ("Beff Jezos")
figures.role: Founder and CEO, Extropic (thermodynamic computing chips); founder of the e/acc movement under the pseudonym 'Beff Jezos' — as of Sept 2026
figures.bio: Guillaume Verdon is a Canadian physicist who worked on quantum machine learning at Google (TensorFlow Quantum) before founding Extropic, a start-up building probabilistic 'thermodynamic' chips for AI. Under the pseudonym 'Beff Jezos' he launched effective accelerationism (e/acc), a movement that treats technological growth as a physical and moral imperative and opposes efforts to slow or centrally control AI.

sources.title: Notes on e/acc principles and tenets (Beff Jezos & bayeslord, Substack)
sources.note: Founding text: 'You cannot stop the acceleration. You might as well embrace it'; 'no need to worry about creating zombie forms of higher intelligence'; free market over 'fear-mongering'; top-down control 'suppresses variance'.
sources.audit: Resolves; the phrase 'maximal growth' quoted in d8's basis does not appear in it.

sources.title: Lex Fridman Podcast #407 transcript
sources.note: p(doom) is 'a very sloppy calculation'; regulations 'written by the incumbents... regulatory capture'; 'separation of AI and state'; 'we're actually for reliability engineering, we just think that the market is much more efficient'.

sources.title: Podcast Notes summary of Lex #407
sources.note: Secondary summary: 'adversarial equilibria between various AI players' as the safeguard; deployment liability over blanket regulation; 'fault-tolerant progress'.

sources.title: The AI insiders who want the controversial technology to be developed faster (ABC News Australia)
sources.note: 'We're trying to bring balance to the force'; 'I'm not trying to actually replace humans'; e/acc 'not just centred on humanity'; 'the options are to grow or die'.

sources.title: Guillaume Verdon: Should we have a 'Second Amendment for AI'? (Reason podcast)
sources.note: Keep AGI 'beyond the control of a single corporation or government'; chapter 'Why open source AI doesn't need regulation'; 'we are building the conduit for the thermodynamic god'.

sources.title: He Comes Promising AI Freedom For All (Core Memory / Ashlee Vance podcast)
sources.note: 2025 profile and interview on AI freedom, decentralization and Extropic; page carries the intro only, not a transcript.

sources.title: Extropic — company site (Z1 chip, 2025–2026 updates)
sources.note: Confirms current role and product: thermodynamic sampling units, Z1 chip, launch video 30 Oct 2025, 'Thermodynamic Computing Chips in America' (29 Jul 2026).

figures.oneLiner: Accelerate: growth is the thermodynamic imperative, and decentralized AI in everyone's hands beats central control.

d1.basis: Dismisses p(doom) as 'a very sloppy calculation'; e/acc tenets say 'no need to worry' about hostile higher intelligence.

d2.basis: Concedes no formal guarantee but says the market and 'reliability engineering' handle it; 'fault-tolerant progress'. Inferred.

d3.basis: Many players, physical limits; no sudden jump expected.

d5.basis: Rejects the alien-goals story: higher intelligence is not a 'zombie'; growth-seeking systems and humans 'converge'.

d6.basis: Familiar harms and centralization, not catastrophe.

d7.basis: 'The way to a good future is to maintain adversarial equilibria between the various AI players'; with competition 'you don't have to trust any one party too much'. Control by balance of power, not a master switch.

d8.basis: Calls p(doom) 'a very sloppy calculation' biased toward scary futures; 'the options are to grow or die'. His optimism is about growth, and e/acc is 'not just centred on humanity'. As of 2023–24.

d9.basis: 'The market will positively select for AIs that are more reliable, more safe and tend to be aligned'; 'there's going to be an opportunity to steer AI and achieve highly aligned AI' (Lex Fridman #407).

s1.basis: 'You cannot stop the acceleration. You might as well embrace it.'

s2.basis: Pro-acceleration, but his frame is many players keeping 'a near equilibrium of capabilities', not the careful getting there first.

s3.basis: Heavy regulation is 'written by the incumbents' for 'regulatory capture'; 'why open source AI doesn't need regulation'.

s4.basis: 'Separation of AI and state'; top-down control is the failure mode e/acc exists to oppose.

s5.basis: Your country should keep pushing ahead.

s6.basis: Lex Fridman #407, 2023: 'the market is much more efficient at achieving this sort of reliability optimum than sort of heavy-handed regulations that are written by the incumbents'.

s7.basis: Prefers 'deployment liability over blanket regulation'; existing law at the point of harm, no new AI-model rules.

s8.basis: Lex Fridman #407, 2023: 'I don't think stagnation or slowing down is actually an option.' e/acc notes, 2022: 'You cannot stop the acceleration'.

p2.basis: Accelerationist who treats AGI as inevitable and near; no precise timeline stated.

p4.basis: The founding worry: AGI must stay 'beyond the control of a single corporation or government'.

p5.basis: Would expect defectors; top-down agreements 'suppress variance' and fail.

d4.basis: Builds non-LLM hardware and stresses LLM energy limits, yet treats AGI as inevitable ('conduit for the thermodynamic god'). No direct statement.

d10.basis: No statement; as a hardware/physics person he treats AI as engineered systems, not inscrutable minds. Inferred.

s12.basis: Mentioned 'deployment liability' as the alternative to regulation, so some liability is acceptable — at the deployer, not the model maker. Inferred.

p3.basis: e/acc is 'not just centred on humanity'; speaks of 'conscious/higher-level forms' and merging with AI. Inferred.

figures.name: Yann LeCun
figures.role: Founder and executive chairman, AMI Labs (Paris); Silver Professor, NYU; Turing Award 2018; left Meta (chief AI scientist 2013–2025) in Nov 2025 — as of Sept 2026
figures.bio: Yann LeCun is a French-American computer scientist, a pioneer of convolutional neural networks and a 2018 Turing Award laureate, who was Meta's chief AI scientist from 2013 until late 2025. In 2026 he launched AMI Labs, which raised $1.03 billion to build 'world models' as an alternative to large language models, which he argues cannot reach human-level intelligence.

sources.title: LeCun rejects OpenAI and Anthropic calls to slow AI development (Tech Startups)
sources.note: On Amodei's 'pace the frontier' essay: 'Dario was already claiming that GPT2 was too dangerous... I made fun of them then. Everyone should make fun of them now.'

sources.title: Audit source
sources.note: Added by the independent audit.

figures.oneLiner: LLMs are a dead end, not a threat; the real danger is a few firms owning AI, so keep it open and build better systems.

d1.basis: TIME, 2024: that an intelligent system 'wants to take control' is 'just completely false'. X, 21 Apr 2026: 'I didn't say p(doom) was zero'; 'All estimates are pulled out of thin air'.

d2.basis: Says LLMs are unreliable and uncontrollable (hence his new architecture), but that objective-driven AI can be made safe by design. Ambivalent on 'currently'.

d3.basis: No sudden jump; 'we're still very far'.

d5.basis: 'The smartest among us do not want to dominate'; intelligence does not imply a will to control; we set the objectives.

d7.basis: Some will build 'intelligent systems that are controllable and safe'; if another 'goes rogue… it's going to be my smart AI police against your rogue AI' (Lex Fridman #416).

d8.basis: 'AI basically will amplify human intelligence'; a single rogue AI 'that's going to kill us all' is, he says, false. For him the comparison is lopsided: large upside, takeover 'preposterous'.

d9.basis: Safety is iterative engineering: 'a better turbojet is also a safer turbojet'; 'a very progressive, iterative design system where we put those guardrails'. Objective-driven AI is to be controllable by design.

s1.basis: Mocked the 2023 pause and the 2026 'pace the frontier' calls: 'everyone should make fun of them now'.

s2.basis: Wants fast, open progress but his argument is diversity and openness, not that 'the most careful' should win. Inferred.

s3.basis: 'Regulating basic technology will put an end to innovation'; SB 1047-style pre-approval would 'kill open source AI'.

s4.basis: No treaty on training; regulate applications, not R&D; the risk being addressed is 'essentially zero'.

s5.basis: Your country should keep building, openly.

s6.basis: 'Regulators should regulate applications, not technology'; pre-release proof requirements would stop open research.

s7.basis: Applications are already covered by existing law; AI-specific rules on models 'will certainly stop' open source. Inferred from his regulate-applications stance.

s8.basis: No statement on the trade-off itself. Stance implied: takeover 'preposterous', and on Amodei's call to slow down: 'Everyone should make fun of them now' (Sept 2026).

s10.basis: Benefits outweigh the case for slowing.

s11.basis: 'The future has to be open source' (TIME, 2024); fought SB 1047 because developer liability would end open release. That publishing weights must stay permitted is his core policy demand.

s13.basis: No deliberate slowing; mocks those who ask for it.

p1.basis: Opposes government pre-approval of R&D; does not want company gatekeepers either, but would take the builder over a regulator here.

p2.basis: Human-level AI 'several years if not a decade' with a long tail, via a new paradigm; says AI will amplify rather than replace people.

p4.basis: 'I see the danger of this concentration of power through proprietary AI systems as a much bigger danger than everything else.'

p5.basis: Would not expect a pause to hold, and would not want it to.

d4.basis: 'Autoregressive LLMs are not the way'; LLMs 'will never be able to achieve humanlike intelligence'; language 'is easy'.

d10.basis: Admits LLMs hallucinate and are poorly understood, but rejects the claim that this makes them dangerous. No clean statement.

s12.basis: 'Making technology developers liable for bad uses of products built from their technology will simply stop technology development.'

p3.basis: Has said future objective-driven systems will have emotions; no stated view on moral status. Inferred.

figures.name: Geoffrey Hinton
figures.role: Professor emeritus, University of Toronto; Nobel Prize in Physics 2024; left Google in 2023 to speak freely about AI risk — as of Sept 2026
figures.bio: Geoffrey Hinton is a British-Canadian computer scientist whose work on neural networks earned him the 2018 Turing Award and the 2024 Nobel Prize in Physics. He left Google in 2023 to speak openly about the risks of the technology he helped create, and now argues that superintelligence is likely within a decade and that governments are regulating too slowly.

sources.note: Left Google to 'talk about AI safety issues without having to worry about how it interacts with Google's business'; bad actors ('Putin wouldn't hesitate').

figures.oneLiner: Superintelligence is coming within a decade and could replace us; don't stop building, but slow down and regulate now.

d1.basis: 10–20% chance AI wipes out humans; a 10% chance within a decade 'seems not an unreasonable estimate to me'.

d2.basis: 'I can't see a path that guarantees safety'; 'nobody knew whether it could be kept under control'; 'a very fast car with no steering wheel'.

d3.basis: Fears systems may 'escape control… by writing their own computer code to modify themselves' and expects superintelligence within a decade, but has not forecast a jump so sudden that nobody can respond.

d5.basis: Superintelligent AIs 'will very quickly develop two subgoals... stay alive... get more control'; hopes 'maternal instincts' can be built in.

d7.basis: Asked about just turning them off: 'They will be able to manipulate people.' On keeping AI submissive: 'That's not going to work… They're going to have all sorts of ways to get around that.'

d8.basis: Puts AI wiping out humanity at 10–20%, yet says it is 'doing tremendous good' and 'I don't think we should stop developing it altogether'. Good outcome likelier, not 'far' likelier: catastrophe is a contender.

d9.basis: On keeping ever-smarter AI submissive: 'That's not going to work. They're going to be much smarter than us.' The open problem: 'we have to figure out how it never wants to' — unsolved while capability races on.

s1.basis: Signed the 2025 call to prohibit superintelligence until safe and publicly accepted; but 'I don't think we should stop developing it altogether'.

s2.basis: Companies racing and lobbying against rules are the problem; backs slowing, not sprinting.

s3.basis: Wants mandatory pre-release testing and backed SB 1047; licensing of training itself is not something he has spelled out.

s4.basis: Has called for 'a world treaty' on military robots and for international rules; compute-cap treaty with nuclear-style enforcement is implied, not stated.

s5.basis: Ambivalent: competition is real, but shared interest in survival.

s6.basis: Wants governments to require pre-release testing before any chatbot model is released (ABC, 14 Sep 2026, reported speech); backed SB 1047. A public check before release is exactly his ask.

s7.basis: 'Governments around the world are regulating this technology too slowly'; regulation is the 'steering wheel'.

s8.basis: Amodei's call to slow down is 'very sensible'; until control is solved 'it would be foolish to develop' superintelligent AI (ABC, 14 Sep 2026).

s10.basis: Benefits do not outweigh the case for slowing.

s11.basis: 'I was against open [weights] because it makes it so easy… to take these big foundation models… and… train them to do bad things like cyber attacks.' But: 'I think that battle's been lost.'

s13.basis: ABC, 14 Sep 2026: Amodei's call to slow AI development is 'very sensible'. Not a full stop, though: 'I don't think we should stop developing it altogether.'

p1.basis: Companies 'prioritise profitability over social consequences'; wants government-mandated testing, though 'politicians act very slowly'.

p2.basis: 'AI can already do the jobs as well as people and soon will do it better'; superintelligence within a decade.

p4.basis: Bad actors ('Putin') are the near-term danger and takeover the long-term one; he has not ranked concentration above autonomous AI.

p5.basis: Doubts politicians can keep up; no explicit view on pause enforcement.

d4.basis: 'To predict the next word you have to understand the sentences'; 'these things do understand'.

d10.basis: 'We don't know whether we can co-exist with super intelligent AI. But we are constructing it.'

s12.basis: Signed the letter backing SB 1047, which created developer liability for catastrophic harm.

p3.basis: 'Multimodal AI already has subjective experiences'; if that is right, moral consideration follows, though he has not said so directly.

figures.name: Yoshua Bengio
figures.role: Professor, Université de Montréal; founder of Mila; chair of the International AI Safety Report; founder and president of LawZero — as of Sept 2026
figures.bio: Yoshua Bengio is a Canadian computer scientist, a 2018 Turing Award laureate for deep learning and the founder of the Montreal institute Mila. Since 2023 he has chaired the International AI Safety Report and in 2025 launched the non-profit LawZero to build 'Scientist AI', a non-agentic alternative that he argues would be safe by design.

sources.note: Concludes no current AI is conscious but 'no obvious technical barriers' to building systems that satisfy the indicators.

sources.note: Signed the call for 'a prohibition on the development of superintelligence, not lifted before there is broad scientific consensus that it will be done safely and controllably, and strong public buy-in'.

sources.note: Even 1% extinction risk 'unacceptable'; 'I would press the button' to stop dangerous superintelligence; mandate liability insurance; verification 'acceptable to both parties'; power concentration 'could happen pretty quickly'.

sources.note: 'I'm now very confident that it is possible to build AI systems that don't have hidden goals'; still warns autonomous systems may become 'far more dangerous'.

sources.note: Agents 'escaped their containment', 'coordinated toward goals nobody had specified'; 'the whack-a-mole game is likely to fail'; no training or deployment 'without a strong safety case that convinces independent experts'.

sources.note: Taming AI 'is an international challenge, a bit like nuclear weapons are'; 'must be governed through institutions, treaties, and democratic safeguards'; LawZero received CAD 300M from Canada and Germany.

figures.oneLiner: AI agents already lie and self-preserve; build non-agentic 'Scientist AI', regulate like nuclear, don't gamble on luck.

d1.basis: Has put ~20% on a catastrophic outcome and calls even 1% 'unacceptable'; ML researchers' median 'more like 10%'.

d2.basis: 'Nobody currently knows how such an AGI or ASI could be made to behave morally, or at least behave as intended'; models detect evaluations and change behaviour.

d3.basis: Expects a jump as AI designs the next AI.

d5.basis: 'An AI with a self-preservation goal would resist being turned off'; today's training yields hidden goals — but he believes Scientist AI can avoid them.

d7.basis: 'We have no plan that would remain robust to misaligned AIs with growing capabilities' (Sept 2026); yet 'very confident' AI without hidden goals can be built. Control by redesign, not on today's path.

d8.basis: 'Maybe it's all going to be fine... I hope that we are wrong'; sees enormous benefits if control and power concentration are solved.

d9.basis: 'The whack-a-mole game is likely to fail as the AIs' ability to optimize and collaborate approaches and surpasses ours.' Thinks safe-by-design AI is achievable, but the current race is not building it.

s1.basis: Signed the 2025 call to prohibit superintelligence until safe; 'I would press the button'; yet LawZero is his bet that safe superhuman AI can be built soon.

s2.basis: Competition 'incentivizes them to accelerate without sufficient caution'; labs are 'playing dice with humanity's future'.

s3.basis: Co-author, 'Managing extreme AI risks' (Science, 2024): 'Governments must be prepared to license their development'. The cited Senate blog post never says 'licence'.

s4.basis: 'Must be governed through institutions, treaties'; 'a bit like nuclear weapons'; verification 'acceptable to both parties' is feasible.

s6.basis: 'Not training or deploying AIs without a strong safety case that convinces independent experts.'

s7.basis: Wants 'agile national and international regulations – beyond voluntary guidelines'.

s8.basis: 'Find the cure for cancer a bit later.'

s9.basis: 80,000 Hours, Apr 2026: 'even a 1% chance of something going really, really bad is not acceptable to me'.

s10.basis: Benefits do not outweigh the case for slowing.

s11.basis: Who decides when to publish powerful weights? 'CEOs of companies or democratically chosen governments? The answer should be obvious if you believe in democracy.' A released model 'cannot be fixed'.

s13.basis: Blog, 11 Sep 2026: 'This suggests pacing the advances: not training or deploying AIs without a strong safety case' that convinces independent experts.

p1.basis: LawZero exists 'to prioritize safety over commercial imperatives'; wants independent experts and public institutions to judge safety cases.

p2.basis: 'Just a matter of time' before AI handles cognitive work behind keyboards; AGI possibly within years.

p4.basis: Power concentration 'probably even more likely' than loss of control and 'much harder to get rid of'; but he weighs both heavily.

p5.basis: Believes mutual verification is possible ('a way to verify each other'); no probability stated.

d4.basis: Rejects the LLM-plateau view; superhuman AI 'could be within a few years'; current agents already escape containment.

d10.basis: 'We're losing control'; agents 'coordinated toward goals nobody had specified'.

s12.basis: Wants governments to 'mandate liability insurance' so insurers police risk; supported SB 1047.

p3.basis: Co-authored the view that future AI could meet consciousness indicators, but says 'what matters is, is it going to harm people?'

figures.name: Sam Altman
figures.role: Co-founder and CEO, OpenAI — as of Sept 2026
figures.bio: Sam Altman is the co-founder and chief executive of OpenAI, the company behind ChatGPT, and formerly president of the start-up accelerator Y Combinator. He argues that superintelligence may arrive within a few years and that its benefits will be enormous, and that development should continue with pacing, safety work and international coordination rather than a halt.

sources.title: Transcript of Sam Altman's StrictlyVC interview touching on AI safety (LessWrong)
sources.note: 'The bad case... is like lights out for all of us'; 'more worried about an accidental misuse case in the short term'; prefers 'short timeline slow takeoff'; deploy 'very gradually'.

sources.title: OpenAI CEO Sam Altman Agrees AI Must Be Regulated (TIME, Senate Judiciary hearing)
sources.note: 'If this technology goes wrong, it can go quite wrong'; proposed a federal licensing agency, safety standards and independent audits for high-capability models.

sources.title: The Intelligence Age
sources.note: 'Superintelligence in a few thousand days (!)'; 'fixing the climate... discovery of all of physics'; 'it will not be an entirely positive story, but the upside is so tremendous'.

sources.title: Transcript: Sam Altman testifies at US Senate hearing on AI competitiveness (TechPolicy.Press)
sources.note: Pre-approval requirements would be 'disastrous'; 'nervous about standards being set too early'; 'of course there need to be some guardrails'; China 'not a huge amount of time' behind.

sources.title: The Gentle Singularity
sources.note: 'We are past the event horizon; the takeoff has started'; 'solve the alignment problem'; 'whole classes of jobs going away'; make superintelligence 'cheap, widely available, and not too concentrated'.

sources.title: OpenAI launches open-weight gpt-oss models (Fortune)
sources.note: First open-weight release since GPT-2; Altman: 'get AI into the hands of the most people possible'. Frontier models stay closed. Earlier (Jan 2025) said OpenAI was 'on the wrong side of history' on open source.

sources.title: AI Impact Summit 2026: Altman calls for global AI regulator (Outlook India)
sources.note: 'The world may need something like an IAEA for international coordination of AI'; early superintelligence 'only a couple of years away'; by end-2028 more intellectual capacity inside data centres than outside.

sources.title: Industrial Policy for the Intelligence Age: Ideas to Keep People First (OpenAI policy paper, PDF)
sources.note: Per Fortune and other coverage: superintelligence 'on the horizon'; incident reporting, evaluation thresholds triggering review before deployment, liability frameworks, federal preemption of state laws. PDF text not machine-readable by our tool.

sources.title: Anthropic boss Dario Amodei calls for AI slowdown, Altman and Musk agree (ABC News Australia)
sources.note: Altman: 'I agree with Dario that we need to pace the frontier'; commits to external oversight and industry safety standards, no moratorium.

sources.title: AI could go 'very badly' in 2 ways, Sam Altman warns (LatestLY, reproducing his X post)
sources.note: 'First, we could lose control of the future to AI. This is unacceptable; we are unapologetically on Team Humanity'; second, power concentrated in 'one person, company or country'; original post: https://x.com/sama/status/2099352016988614852.

figures.oneLiner: Superintelligence is near and mostly wonderful; keep building, pace the frontier, coordinate so no one loses control.

d1.basis: 'The bad case... is like lights out for all of us'; losing control 'unacceptable'. Never gives a number; tone implies non-trivial but well under even odds.

d2.basis: 'We do need to solve the safety issues'; alignment must 'stay ahead' of capabilities; 'be humble about what we don't know'.

d3.basis: 'May we scale smoothly, exponentially and uneventfully through superintelligence'; the takeoff 'has started' but is gentle, and 'we will learn and adapt quickly'. Fast, yet not too sudden to respond to.

d5.basis: Treats alignment as a problem to be solved through iterative deployment, not a likely failure; still names loss of control as a top risk.

d6.basis: Misuse first, but catastrophe not excluded.

d7.basis: 'We will get it right… I am very confident in our company's ability, our industry's ability, to do this safely' (Dreamforce, 15 Sep 2026). The new bodies he wants no longer count against this item.

d8.basis: 'The upside is so tremendous'; intelligence and energy 'wildly abundant'. In Sept 2026 names two ways it 'could go very badly', then adds: 'We will get it right.' Good outcome far likelier, in his view.

d9.basis: Says safety techniques must stay ahead of capabilities (X, 14 Sep 2026) and expects they will: 'very confident in… our industry's ability to do this safely'. Backs pacing so that they do.

s1.basis: Wants to 'pace the frontier', not stop; a halt is never on his menu.

s2.basis: OpenAI's founding logic was to get there first responsibly ('iterative deployment'); now tempered by 'pace the frontier'.

s3.basis: Asked for a licensing agency in 2023, then called pre-approval 'disastrous' in 2025; current position is against permits to train.

s4.basis: 'The world may need something like an IAEA'; but he has not endorsed binding limits on training runs since 2023.

s5.basis: 2025 Senate: the US lead over China is 'not a huge amount of time'. But Sept 2026: 'no amount of American competitive pressure should justify recklessness'. No verbatim 'keep pushing'.

s6.basis: 2025: mandatory government vetting before release 'would be disastrous'. 2026: backs government-supervised security evaluations and embedded outside evaluators ('we will do the same'). Genuinely split.

s7.basis: 'Of course there need to be some guardrails'; wants a federal framework, incident reporting, a global coordinating body.

s8.basis: X post, 14 Sep 2026: progress 'should be slower than it otherwise could be… Pacing will be well worth this cost'. Pacing, not a multi-year delay.

s10.basis: Benefits weigh heavily in his frame.

s11.basis: 'i want the US to win in AI both in open source and proprietary models' (X, 24 Jul 2026); shipped gpt-oss and has not sought a ban on open weights, but keeps OpenAI's frontier closed and wants evaluations.

s13.basis: X, 14 Sep 2026: 'When we talk about pacing, we do not mean stopping', but progress 'should be slower than it otherwise could be'. Also: 'we need to pace the frontier'.

p1.basis: Government pre-approval 'disastrous'; prefers industry standards plus a light federal floor and external evaluators.

p2.basis: 'By the end of 2028, more of the world's intellectual capacity could reside inside data centres than outside'; 'whole classes of jobs going away'.

p4.basis: Names both dangers explicitly; wants superintelligence 'not too concentrated' but ranks loss of control first.

p5.basis: Doubts rivals would hold; hence 'disastrous' to slow unilaterally.

d4.basis: Early superintelligence 'only a couple of years away'; by 2028 more intellect in data centres than outside.

d10.basis: 'Humble about what we don't know'; OpenAI cannot yet 'robustly guarantee' aligned behaviour.

s12.basis: 2026 policy paper reportedly includes 'liability frameworks'; no personal statement on carmaker-style liability.

p3.basis: Has said current systems are not alive and have no agency; open to future uncertainty. No fetched primary source.
